stocks.name: Adobe
stocks.text: Used as his example of the market getting software wrong. After AI fears knocked the stock down (36% in a year, 63% from its 2024 high, per the interviewer), he argues that being able to write code quickly does not put Adobe or Photoshop out of business, because software is far more than coding. In his view the advantage goes to incumbents, who can use AI to cut costs. He says the market "has gotten it wrong" on vertical software, and he treats the selloff in hated, unloved software names as a place to look.
stocks.value: No number given. His argument is that the selloff (36% in a year, 63% from the 2024 high, per the interviewer) prices Adobe as if AI makes software worthless.

stocks.name: Alpha Metallurgical Resources
stocks.text: One of his coal bets. He moved from thermal coal (CONSOL) to metallurgical coal, which he found even more favorable, and now holds Alpha and Warrior. He holds Alpha up as his example of an "uber-cannibal": it bought back 32% of its shares in four years, more than Apple (11%) or Microsoft (10%), by putting its spare cash into the stock. He is open that the coal bets can fail, with low-probability things that could go wrong, but calls them favorable bets, part of a group where he does not need every one to work.
stocks.paid: Not stated per share.
stocks.value: In SumZero (Jun 2025) he says the met-coal assets would cost $10–20 billion to build and could be bought for about $2 billion. Alpha bought back 32% of its shares in four years.

stocks.name: Alphabet and Amazon
stocks.text: Named as great "spawners," companies that create new businesses, one of his models for finding compounders. He also tells how Nick Sleep's fund let Amazon grow to roughly 80% of the portfolio and still came out ahead of nearly everyone, as an illustration of letting a winner run. He doesn't say he owns either.
stocks.value: In 2015 he cited Amazon at about 576 times earnings as an example of a frothy valuation. By 2026 he says Amazon is "just starting" (roughly $1 trillion revenue, $3 trillion market cap) and calls it, with Alphabet, a spawner. He never says he owns either.

stocks.name: American Express
stocks.text: Included among the businesses with a moat that he would not sell "unless egregiously overpriced," a bar he says AmEx does not currently meet. He retells Buffett's 1964 bet, putting 40% of his fund into the company after the salad-oil scandal knocked the stock down, because the core moat, trust in the card, was intact.
stocks.paid: Buffett put 40% of his partnership into it after the 1964 salad-oil scandal; he cites the stock at about $70 in 2015.
stocks.value: He says AmEx should be held unless egregiously overpriced, which it is not. His 2002 view: even blue chips like AmEx should be valued on 10 years of free cash flow, sold at 10x in year 10, then halved for margin of safety.

stocks.name: Coca-Cola
stocks.text: A prime example of a brand moat: he lists it with Costco, Visa, Mastercard and AmEx as businesses you hold unless they become egregiously overpriced, which he says they are not now. He cites it as Berkshire's longest-held stock (since 1988, 38 years) and a model for the buy-and-hold discipline he wants investors to adopt earlier in life. He also contrasts a Coke bottler in Turkey with a Pepsi bottler in India, the same business trading at very different prices.
stocks.paid: Buffett paid about $6 a share (split-adjusted) in 1987–88, $1.2 billion for about 6% of the company and 25% of Berkshire's book value.
stocks.value: His 2002 Mosaic article says the whole company could be bought for under $20 billion in 1988 while the brand alone was worth over $100 billion. He notes Coke traded at 40–45x earnings in 2000 and returned under 3% a year from 2000 to 2018. In 2021 he said it is worth more than 15x trailing earnings, maybe 25–30x, and that a purchase at 5x would be a no-brainer.

stocks.name: CONSOL Energy
stocks.text: His entry into coal. He found it after a post on X noted that David Einhorn's CONSOL bet looked like his own 2003–04 IPSCO trade: the company forward-sold its coal inside a price band, so future cash flows were visible and the risk-reward was favorable. He later switched the thermal-coal bet to metallurgical coal (Alpha and Warrior), which he found even more attractive.
stocks.paid: Not stated per share. The company had a market cap near $1.8 billion in early 2024.
stocks.value: Its coal is forward-sold a year ahead inside a price band, so the cash flow is largely known. It put 100% of discretionary cash flow into buybacks after cancelling the dividend. He compared it to IPSCO.

stocks.name: Constellation Software
stocks.text: A major position in his Wagons fund and the stock he talks about most. He calls it a rare company, and says that in many ways it is superior to Berkshire: it buys only one kind of business, small vertical software companies, through a delegated model where deal teams can close purchases up to $20 million without approval. He describes a machine reinvesting at about 25% and growing cash flow 20–25% a year, with founder Mark Leonard's culture passed down to the units. It compounded around 35% a year for about 15 years. He says AI fears took the stock "out back and shot" and that the market is wrong that cloners can replace this software, and that is when he got interested. He criticizes fund managers who trim it at 10% of the portfolio.

stocks.name: Gimat (Turkey's "Costco")
stocks.paid: He met the owner, visited both stores and bought when the market cap was about $70 million against about $70 million of surplus real estate, so "the business was free". The funds now own over 30%. The date of purchase and price per share are not stated.
stocks.value: His daughter Monsoon Pabrai pitched it at Best Ideas 2026 (MOI Global, Mar 20, 2026) at a market cap of about $156 million against an intrinsic value of about $175 million, from about $11 million of profit after tax at 10x plus $50 million of projected office sales and rental property valued at a 6.5% yield. Her framing was "heads I win, tails I don't lose too much".
stocks.text: An Ankara wholesaler and hypermarket (GMTAS, Borsa Istanbul) that grew out of a cooperative of more than 1,000 wholesalers. It has two stores that are mobbed with customers, with no parking; the flagship does about $1,200 of sales per square foot at gross margins above 20%. It sells in bulk at low margins and owns its real estate, which hedges Turkish inflation. About 99% of the shares are free float, and the general manager holds proxies for over 25% of the wholesalers. Net margins are thin at 1–2%. He calls it almost a venture investment with few "tread marks", and in April 2026 said 70% of his portfolio was in three Turkish stocks. It is also a top-five holding of the Wagons ETF (5.8% at Oct 31, 2026).

funds.name: Pabrai Investment Funds
funds.summary: The original funds. Pabrai started them in July 1999 with $1 million from eight friends, plus $100,000 of his own, and copied the Buffett partnerships of the 1950s and 60s: no management fee, a 6% annual hurdle with one-fourth of gains above it going to him, redemptions once a year, and no public disclosure of holdings. He runs a handful of concentrated bets and says the structure gives him long-term investors. It is a family of partnerships, including an offshore fund, and minimums are in the millions.
funds.size: About $1.4 billion in total across the private funds and the ETF (Oct 31, 2026). Subtracting the ETF's $313 million implies roughly $1.1 billion in the private funds, though he does not break this out.
funds.holdings: The funds do not publish holdings. From his 2026 talks, the main positions are Reysas, the Turkish warehouse company, where the funds own about 41% and which was 40% of the offshore fund in 2023; Gimat, the Turkish "Costco" (over 30% owned); Constellation Software; the coal companies Alpha Metallurgical and Warrior Met Coal; the offshore drillers Transocean and Valaris; TAV Airports; and Kaspi.kz. See the stock list below for prices and his reasoning.
performance: About 12.9% a year after fees from July 1, 1999 through September 30, 2024, against 7.8% for the S&P 500 with dividends (Forbes, Nov 2024).
$100,000 at inception grew to $1.83 million by December 2023, a gain of over 12% a year against about 7% for the S&P 500 (University of Nebraska Omaha introduction, May 2024).
Earlier checkpoints from event introductions: $889,000 at the end of 2015; about $1.4 million by March 2021 (13% a year).
The first year was up over 70%, when assets were about $2.5 million (Georgetown, Mar 2021).
I could not find published returns for 2025 or 2026. The private funds do not publish them, so recent performance of the private funds is not available here.

funds.name: Pabrai Wagons ETF (NYSE Arca: WAGN)
funds.kind: Actively managed ETF, open to anyone
funds.started: Predecessor mutual fund began Sept 29, 2023; ETF trading began Feb 9, 2026
funds.summary: A long-only, concentrated, actively managed fund of small and mid-cap companies around the world, with Pabrai as sole portfolio manager. It began as the Pabrai Wagons Fund (a mutual fund) and was converted into an ETF in February 2026, keeping the same manager, strategy and track record (the institutional class). The name comes from "circling the wagons" around his highest-conviction ideas. The fee is a single 0.90%. He said he created it because the private funds' minimums are too high for most people who wanted to invest with him. The fund has no overlap with the S&P 500.
funds.size: Net assets $313.0 million, 20 holdings, weighted average market cap $6.3 billion, median $2.8 billion (Oct 31, 2026).

holdingsTable.note: Top ten are 67.4% of assets. By sector: energy 24.7%, real estate 14.9%, information technology 14.3%, financials 13.6%, industrials 12.3%, materials 11.4%, consumer staples 5.8%, consumer discretionary 2.9%. The fund describes about 82% of the portfolio as six themes: offshore oil services, Reysas, the Constellation Software family, Edelweiss, U.S. met coal and TAV. At March 31, 2026 it also held Alpha Metallurgical, Kaspi.kz, Topicus, Lumine, Danaos, Mongolian Mining, TAB Gida, Nuvama and Sygnity.

performance: As of Oct 31, 2026: up 30.14% year to date and 34.30% over one year (NAV), against 11.77% and 12.11% for the S&P 500. Since inception (Sept 29, 2023) it has returned 16.91% a year against 21.83% for the S&P 500.

As of Sept 30, 2026: up 21.70% year to date, 29.28% over one year, and 14.84% a year since inception, against 22.87% for the S&P 500. October added almost 7% after September fell 8%, so returns swing widely.
2024 was +10.91%. Through Dec 31, 2024 it was up 15.42% since inception, against 30.48% for the S&P 500. It was down 2.12% for 2025 through Sept 30.
In short, it has trailed the S&P 500 since inception but has led it sharply over the last year. Three years is a short record for a concentrated fund.
